clue.text: Regulators behind bars providing scientific study

blocks.note: first meaning: the upside-down dispensers fixed to spirit bottles in a pub, which measure out each shot
second meaning: the branch of physics dealing with light and vision

explanation.surface: Prison guards or wardens supplying material for a piece of research.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind bars' suggests prison, but these bars are pub counters; an optic is the British name for the measuring spout on an upturned spirit bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: The physics of light and lenses is a named science, and pub measuring devices share its plural name.

clue.text: Officer in charge of feeding European prisoners on board

indicators.note: to feed something is to put it inside, so one piece goes into another
in a down answer, one thing sitting on another is written above it

blocks.note: IC is the standard abbreviation for in charge
a Pole is a person from Poland
cons is slang for convicts
a board is a table, as in board and lodging

explanation.surface: A prison ship's officer is responsible for feeding the European inmates held aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Officer in charge' reads as one rank, but only 'Officer' defines. In a down answer, 'on' puts the prisoners above the board.
explanation.definitionFit: A constable is the lowest-ranking British police officer, so the rank is a specific example of an officer.

clue.text: Nudged, I retain disinclination to move

indicators.note: something nudged is pushed out of position, so the letters get moved around

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who, even when prodded, stays stubbornly reluctant to get going.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost a definition of the answer itself: being nudged and not moving is exactly what the word describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Physics and everyday speech both use the word for a body's tendency to stay at rest or resist change.

clue.text: Exhibit involving cow and sheep, Hirst's second

indicators.note: to involve is literally to roll up or entangle, so the letters are tangled together
the second item in a word is its second letter, and only that one is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the second letter of the artist's surname

explanation.surface: A gallery exhibit featuring a cow and a sheep, recalling Damien Hirst's animals preserved in formaldehyde.
explanation.walkthrough: Hirst really did exhibit a pickled cow and a sheep, so the surface seems factual; the animals are just letters to be tangled with the I.
explanation.definitionFit: A showpiece is an item put on display as a prime example, which is exactly what an exhibit is.

clue.text: Mother's daughter flees religious slaughter

indicators.note: whoever flees leaves the scene, so that letter goes missing

blocks.note: MA is mother, with the possessive S
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
sacred means holy or religious

explanation.surface: A girl escapes persecution as her family faces a sectarian massacre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flees' looks like part of the story, but it only tells the daughter's letter to leave the word for religious.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name the brutal killing of many people at once, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Staff car JR scratched in American capital

indicators.note: a runner that is scratched is withdrawn from a race, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: to staff a post is to man it
a Jaguar is a make of car
taken as written: the two letters to remove

explanation.surface: A staff car belonging to someone called JR has been scratched while parked in a US city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American capital' suggests Washington, but the Americas include Central America. 'Scratched' removes two letters that are not next to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Managua is the capital city of Nicaragua, a country in Central America, so it is an American capital in the wider sense.

clue.text: President's taken over, throwing master off jet

indicators.note: something taken over is flipped over, so it reads the other way in this down answer
throwing something off gets rid of it, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: Donald Trump, US president, with the possessive S
M is the standard abbreviation for master

explanation.surface: A president has seized power and thrown the pilot off his jet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet' pretends to be an aircraft; it is a gush of liquid. TRUMPS read upwards is SPMURT, and dropping M leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A jet of water and a spurt of water are both a sudden forceful stream, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: No winner's too stretched

blocks.note: too and also both mean in addition
a road that stretches somewhere runs there, so stretched is ran

explanation.surface: A complaint that nobody wins because everyone has been pushed too far.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse-racing results once listed unplaced horses under 'also ran', so the term means a loser or also-competitor.

clue.text: New student in resort finds means of getting up to date

definitions.text: means of getting up to date

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: a fresher is a British term for a first-year university student
a last resort is a last recourse

explanation.surface: A new student at a holiday resort discovers a way to catch up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' suggests a seaside town, but it means recourse, a thing turned to for help.
explanation.definitionFit: A short course that updates people's professional knowledge is the standard way to bring skills up to date.

clue.text: Crystalline mineral cast down toilet

blocks.note: someone cast down is sad or blue
john is slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: A crystal has been thrown down the lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast down' looks like throwing, but it is the adjective meaning dejected. Blue John is a banded fluorite mined only in Castleton, Derbyshire, in England.
explanation.definitionFit: This rare purple-and-yellow fluorspar is a crystalline mineral prized for ornaments.

clue.text: Where peacekeepers send their reserves, based on dodgy evidence?

blocks.note: UN peacekeeping forces are sent to conflict zones
a safe is where valuables held in reserve are kept

explanation.surface: A question about where UN troops dispatch reinforcements, with doubts about the intelligence behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'the UN's safe': the place the UN would put its reserves. An unsafe verdict in British law is one a court of appeal overturns as unreliable.
explanation.definitionFit: A conviction is called unsafe when the evidence supporting it is unreliable, so the word describes a judgment built on shaky proof.

clue.text: Last of dogs with docked tail

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: final letter of the word
to dock a tail is to cut it short

explanation.surface: The final dog in a line is the one whose tail has been docked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docked tail' reads as a phrase, but 'docked' is the wordplay and 'tail' the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the short upright tail of a rabbit, hare or deer.

clue.text: Riveting work that could make servant spit

blocks.note: a page is a boy servant
a roasting spit is something that turns the meat

explanation.surface: A book so gripping it would make a servant spit in outrage or excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riveting' suggests metalwork, and 'spit' a rude servant; the spit is the kitchen roasting rod, which turns.
explanation.definitionFit: A book so compelling that readers keep flipping onwards is called by this name, so it is a gripping read.

clue.text: Old church keeps back wine aplenty for duration of festival

indicators.note: whatever keeps something holds it inside
going back means running the opposite way

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
CE is the Church of England
a vat holds wine in great quantity

explanation.surface: An ancient church stores plenty of wine to last the whole feast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duration of festival' sounds vague, but the church calendar has a precise term for the eight days after a feast.
explanation.definitionFit: In the church calendar an octave is the eight-day period following a major feast, the span over which it is celebrated.

clue.text: Drink consumed by Arabs, in theory

indicators.note: something consumed is swallowed up inside, so the answer lies within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: A remark that, in principle, some drink is consumed by Arabs.
explanation.walkthrough: The irony is that alcohol would be frowned on by many Arabs, so 'in theory' reads naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: Absinthe is a strong green aniseed-flavoured spirit, a kind of alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Sports venue broadcasting darts news  …

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter seed widely, so the letters are strewn about

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sports arena is showing the latest darts news, and the ellipsis leads into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadcasting and darts news belong together, which hides the anagram. St Andrews is a Scottish town, the home of golf.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Course in this Scottish town regularly hosts golf's Open Championship, so it is a famous sporting venue.

clue.text: Footwear all kids initially held in derision

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters, one from each word
something held in is enclosed by the surrounding piece

blocks.note: first letters of the two words
sneers are expressions of derision

explanation.surface: A certain style of shoe that every child mocked at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' seems to mean at first, but it picks the first letters of 'all kids', which sit inside SNEERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sneakers are the American word for soft rubber-soled sports shoes, a type of footwear.

clue.text: …  report of a barbarous gathering

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: barbarous means cruel

explanation.surface: Following on from the previous clue, a news report about a violent crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'a cruel' quickly and it matches the answer. 'Gathering' suggests a crowd but means accumulation.
explanation.definitionFit: An accrual is a building up or accumulating over time, as interest gathers on a loan.

clue.text: £1 among loose coins used for chips?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the material; the answer is a noun

indicators.note: whatever is among something sits in its midst
something loose has come apart and can be rearranged

blocks.note: the pound sign comes from L for libra
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pound among some loose change, spent in the chip shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The chips are potato chips on the surface but microchips in the answer, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Integrated circuits in computers are made on wafers of this semiconductor element, so it is the chipmakers' material.

clue.text: Arrange completely powerless travel document

indicators.note: completely without power means every P, the physics abbreviation for power, is removed

blocks.note: a passport is the document needed to cross borders

explanation.surface: A useless travel document that no longer grants any entry.
explanation.walkthrough: Both P's must go, not just one, which is why 'completely' is there.
explanation.definitionFit: To assort things is to sort or classify them into groups, which is to arrange them.

clue.text: Dish to get the runners moving?

blocks.note: first meaning: the first course of a meal
second meaning: the official who fires the gun to begin a race

explanation.surface: A meal that gives people the runs.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second definition as a description rather than a synonym; 'runners' also hints at the gut.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an appetiser course and the race official whose signal sends competitors off.

clue.text: Spoilt deck shuffled and put in store

indicators.note: cards that are shuffled change their order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A damaged pack of cards is shuffled and then put away in a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shuffled' belongs so naturally with 'deck' that it hides its job.
explanation.definitionFit: To stockpile is to accumulate a reserve of supplies, so the past tense means stored away.

clue.text: Junior's favourite toy's lost its stuffing

indicators.note: losing the stuffing empties the middle, leaving only the outer shell

blocks.note: a teacher's pet is a favourite
a teddy is a stuffed toy; only its first and last letters remain

explanation.surface: A child's beloved soft toy has split open and lost its filling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Junior' looks like a child's name, but it is the definition, and the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Petty means minor or lower in rank, as in a petty officer, the junior naval rank.

clue.text: Book? English author gets nothing for one

indicators.note: one thing given for another is swapped in its place

blocks.note: Kingsley or Martin Amis, English novelists
O looks like zero
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An English writer is asked about a book and earns nothing for one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' pairs naturally with an author, but here it is a book of the Bible; O replaces the I in AMIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Amos is one of the minor prophets of the Old Testament, whose book appears in the Bible.

clue.text: Unexpected point concluding a second-rate game

indicators.note: something concluding comes at the end, so it is placed after the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
B grade is second-rate
RU is rugby union
PT is the abbreviation for point

explanation.surface: A surprise final point at the end of a poor match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' comes first in the clue but last in the answer, because 'concluding' sends it to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrupt change is sudden and without warning, so it is unexpected.

clue.text: Being right to worry, with smoke closing in

indicators.note: something closing in surrounds what lies within

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
what's eating you means what's worrying you
to cure fish or meat is to preserve it, often by smoking

explanation.surface: Someone is justified in feeling anxious as smoke advances on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being right' reads as a phrase, but 'Being' is the noun definition; smoke is the verb, as in smoked salmon.
explanation.definitionFit: A creature is any living thing, and a being is the same, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Christian playing partners no golfer's backing

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: West and East are partners at the bridge table
nay is an old word for no
Ernie Els is a South African golfer

explanation.surface: A Christian man playing golf with partners but without any golfer's support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing partners' suggests golf, but these are bridge partners, named by compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: A Wesleyan is a Methodist following John Wesley's teaching, so a member of a Christian denomination.

clue.text: Ice in fixed form circling globe

indicators.note: to circle something is to go all the way round it

blocks.note: set means firm or fixed in shape
an orb is a sphere or globe

explanation.surface: Ice frozen into a solid shape around a sphere, like a snow globe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ice' reads as frozen water but is a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A water ice is a frozen fruit dessert, and sorbet is the usual name for it.
